title: Confront Your Dark Side: The Law of Repression
coreMove: Treat projection and overreaction as evidence of a disowned trait, then integrate the energy instead of acting it out sideways.
sourcePressure: This law says disowned traits do not disappear; they leak through projection, overreaction, moralizing, contradiction, and scapegoating.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Making the shadow theatrical darkness rather than ordinary traits the self-image refuses to own.

exampleSpecs.domain: a vegan cafe owner furious at a supplier's ambition to expand
exampleSpecs.audience: an entrepreneur whose own ambition is disguised as moral purity
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a useful partnership is destroyed by projection
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she reviews the meeting and sees her harshest accusation lands exactly where she has been secretly wanting scale
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a supplier catalog folded beside a tray of unsold pastries

exampleSpecs.domain: a museum docent condemning a teenager's need for attention
exampleSpecs.audience: a retired performer whose old hunger has gone underground

exampleSpecs.firstImage: a velvet rope beside a glass case of stage costumes

exampleSpecs.domain: a corporate ethics officer obsessed with a colleague's small rule bending

exampleSpecs.audience: an artist denying her own impatience with slow craft

exampleSpecs.domain: a neighborhood mediator who keeps calling one resident aggressive

sourceAnchors.name: Richard Nixon
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses Nixon to show a public persona of discipline and control undermined by denied insecurity, hostility, and paranoia
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Nixon could read power and still fail to read the shadow operating inside his own calculations.

sourceAnchors.name: Carl Jung
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses Jung's shadow framework to explain how disowned traits remain active through projection and eruption
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Jung gives the hidden material a name so it can stop making decisions in the dark.
